title: SNL’s Weekend Update Roasts Trump After He Misses Out on Nobel Peace Prize Victory
body:
The latest episode of “Saturday Night Live” turned its trademark “Weekend Update” segment into a sharp‑tongued roast of former President Donald Trump after the Nobel Committee formally withdrew his nomination for the Peace Prize. Co‑anchor Colin Jost seized the moment, quipping that the snub felt “like thinking you might win an Oscar for ‘Tom & Jerry,’” a line that quickly became the night’s most‑repeated meme on social media. The joke, nestled among a series of missteps that plagued the show’s opening half, underscored how the comedy program continues to use political satire as a barometer for current events.

The segment arrived after a notoriously uneven cold open, in which host Shane Gillis stumbled through a monologue that failed to land with the studio audience. Gillis’s attempts at topical humor—including a cringe‑inducing slip that produced an accidental expletive during a Dr. Seuss‑themed sketch—set a low bar that “Weekend Update” promptly aimed to raise. Jost’s Trump punchline, however, resonated because it tapped into a broader cultural conversation about the former president’s lingering quest for validation from elite institutions. By framing the Nobel withdrawal as a cinematic disappointment, the sketch highlighted the absurdity of Trump’s self‑styled “global peacemaker” narrative, a narrative that has repeatedly collided with diplomatic realities.

The joke also fits within a longer tradition of “SNL” using the “Weekend Update” desk as a platform for political commentary. Since the show’s inception, the segment has evolved from simple news parody to a more incisive, sometimes biting, analysis of the week’s headlines. In recent years, the desk has become a launchpad for jokes about Trump’s legal battles, his social media bans, and his influence on the Republican Party. This week’s Nobel gag reinforced that pattern, suggesting that the comedy troupe sees the former president’s desire for accolades as increasingly out of step with public perception. Critics have praised the line for its succinctness, noting that it distills a complex controversy into a single, relatable analogy.

The reaction from viewers and commentators was swift. Twitter lit up with the hashtag #NobelSnub, with many users sharing Jost’s line alongside clips of the segment. Some political pundits argued that the joke reflected a growing consensus that Trump’s claims to global statesmanship are more theatrical than substantive. Others, however, cautioned against conflating satire with factual assessment, reminding audiences that the Nobel Committee’s decision was based on procedural criteria rather than a direct indictment of Trump’s policies. Still, the humor’s viral spread illustrates how comedy can shape the public narrative surrounding high‑profile political figures.

Behind the scenes, “SNL” producers acknowledged the mixed reception to the opening monologue but defended the decision to keep the “Weekend Update” segment edgy. In a post‑show interview, head writer Bryan Tucker explained that the team deliberately leaned into “over‑the‑top” jokes to counterbalance the earlier misfires, aiming to restore the show’s rhythm before the commercial break. The strategy appears to have worked, as the segment’s ratings saw a modest uptick compared to the previous week, suggesting that audiences remain hungry for pointed political satire even when the surrounding material falters.

Looking ahead, the episode may signal a renewed emphasis on political lampooning as the 2024 election cycle intensifies. With Trump positioning himself once again as a potential candidate, “SNL” is likely to keep the former president in its crosshairs, using humor to dissect his every move—from campaign rallies to potential legal outcomes. Whether the show can consistently blend sharp wit with solid comedic timing remains to be seen, but the Nobel joke proved that a single well‑crafted line can reignite the conversation and remind viewers that satire still holds a potent place in the national discourse.
